title: No one to blame
hookLine: after his last meal, the Buddha tells Ananda no one should blame Cunda who cooked it
last: DECAY IS INHERENT IN ALL COMPONENT THINGS.

cards: A meal goes wrong. In the long account of the Buddha's final journey, he stops at the mango grove of a smith named Cunda. Cunda cooks for him and his monks, glad to have them.
After eating, the Buddha falls badly sick, with sharp pains, and still walks on toward the place where he will die.
Somewhere behind him is a cook about to hear that the last meal he served his teacher came just before the sickness. What does the Buddha do about the cook?

teach.b: First, the dish. Before the meal, the text says, the Buddha asked Cunda to serve one particular dish only to him, and to bury whatever was left, because he saw no one else who could digest it.
Readers still argue about what that dish was. Whatever it was, he kept the monks away from it. Second, the danger.

Later, sick on the road, the Buddha tells Ananda, his attendant, that someone might stir up remorse in Cunda: telling him it was his loss, his fault, that the teacher died after eating his food. Third, the message.
The Buddha asks Ananda to go to Cunda and say something else.

Two offerings of food, he says, bear the same great fruit, above all others: the meal a Buddha eats before his awakening, and the meal he eats before his final passing. Cunda's meal isn't to be remembered as a mistake.
It is named a gift. Fourth, what this does. The sutta doesn't hide the order of events; the meal and the sickness sit side by side in the text.
Buddhist teaching is full of causes.

teach.h: A CAUSE IS NOT A CULPRIT.
teach.b: But here the Buddha won't let a cause become a culprit, and he spends some of his last strength on a cook's peace of mind.
When someone dies, grief looks for a place to land: the doctor, the driver, the sister who didn't call, ourselves.
Blame offers one. This story offers another: what happened, held without a verdict.

how: Buddhists remember Cunda's meal in retellings of the Buddha's last days, and the Buddha's message to him is read as a teaching on compassion and on not turning grief into blame.

o: a wealthy patron who built the Buddha a monastery
the Buddha's attendant who went aside alone to weep
the smith who cooked the Buddha's last meal, spared all blame

games.q: who's who in the last meal — tap the pairs.
p: the smith who cooked the meal
served only to the Buddha, the rest buried

s: the Buddha told Ananda to keep the news from Cunda
he sent Ananda to Cunda with a message, so remorse wouldn't take hold.
the sutta says two offerings of food bear the same great fruit
the meal before a Buddha's awakening and the meal before his final passing.
everyone agrees what the special dish was
readers still argue about it; the text names it, but the meaning is disputed.

games.q: you're Ananda. your teacher is sick after Cunda's meal, and people may start to talk. what does the Buddha ask you to do?
o: go to Cunda and tell him his meal was a gift of great fruit.
warn other hosts to be careful with food.
games.why: he sends Ananda to Cunda. two offerings bear equal fruit, he says, and Cunda's is one of them. a dying man protects the cook.

practice: Let one blame come to mind, something small is fine: a late delivery, a coworker's slip, something you've been holding against yourself.
Breathe in and name what happened, plainly, the way the sutta names the meal and then the sickness; breathe out and set down the word fault, just for now.
You aren't deciding that nobody was responsible, only letting the event be an event.

wordCard.voice: Cunda, the cook who served the Buddha's last meal and was told to carry no remorse: a cause is not a culprit. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: held without a verdict. Cunda's meal was named a gift. That's day seven hundred sixty-seven.
